Growth proceeds steadily under the warm thermal regimes typical of its native habitat, with water temperatures consistently in the range of 27 °C [T = 27 °C] during the primary growing season. The newly hatched yolk-sac larva is extremely small, with a wet weight at birth of merely 0.0018 grams [Wwb = 0.0018 grams]; this minuscule mass reflects the modest diameter of the fertilised ovum, which measures roughly 1.5 millimeters across. Such a small starting size imposes a brief window of endotrophic dependency before the larva must transition to exogenous feeding, a trophic switch that typically occurs soon after the absorption of the yolk reserves is complete.

Sexual maturation in this species is tied to the attainment of a specific body size rather than age alone, and field surveys indicate that puberty begins once individuals reach approximately 5 centimeters [Lp = approximately 5 centimeters] in total length. The onset of gonadal activity marks a significant physiological transition; prior to this point, juveniles allocate resources primarily to somatic growth, but once the threshold is crossed, energy begins to be diverted toward gametogenesis and reproductive preparation. The length at puberty represents roughly 43 percent of the ultimate total length, suggesting that C. walkeri follows a pattern of delayed maturation common among iteroparous freshwater catfishes that face moderate levels of predation. Adult females are capable of sustained reproductive output, and detailed observations of captive stock held at a stable temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C] have allowed researchers to quantify the maximum reproductive rate. Each gravid female produces a single clutch per spawning event [F_R_i = single clutch per spawning event], with fecundity averaging approximately 222 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 222 eggs per clutch], a figure derived from the maximum daily reproduction rate of approximately 0.608 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 0.608 eggs per day].

At the upper end of the size spectrum, adult Walker catfish attain an ultimate wet weight of 16 grams [Wwi = 16 grams], a figure that corresponds closely with predictions from the length-mass relationship established for the species. This maximum adult body mass is modest compared to that of larger claroteid congeners such as Chrysichthys auratus, which can exceed several hundred grams, but it appears well-suited to the relatively shallow, food-limited streams that C. walkeri inhabits. The ultimate total length of 11.5 centimeters [Li = 11.5 centimeters] is itself at the lower end of the genus range. Growth rates slow appreciably after sexual maturity, with most individuals approaching their asymptotic dimensions within the first two to three years of life. The species exhibits a typical teleost growth trajectory, with rapid length gain during the juvenile phase followed by a pronounced deceleration once reproductive allocation begins. Longitudinal recapture data from a mark-recapture study in the Bandama River basin suggest that the majority of somatic expansion occurs before the fish reach their pubertal length, after which energy is diverted increasingly to gamete production and spawning migrations.

Longevity records for C. walkeri indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 6.5 years [am = approximately 6.5 years] under the thermal conditions of its natural environment, where water temperatures average 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This lifespan is moderate relative to other members of the family Claroteidae, some of which may live for a decade or more in stable lacustrine habitats. The species appears to be reproductively active throughout much of its adult life, with iteroparous spawning bouts occurring seasonally in synchrony with the onset of local rains. Natural mortality is highest during the early larval and post-settlement juvenile stages, when predation from larger piscivores and invertebrate predators takes a heavy toll. Older individuals experience senescence-related declines in condition factor and reproductive output, and very few fish survive beyond the sixth year. The combination of a relatively short lifespan and a high reproductive rate suggested by the maximum daily reproduction rate of approximately 0.608 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 0.608 eggs per day] positions this species toward the opportunistic end of the slow-fast continuum, a pattern consistent with small-bodied catfishes occupying variable, disturbance-prone riverine environments.

Comparative physiological analyses place C. walkeri within the expected range for a tropical claroteid of its body size. The maximum recorded annual reproductive output, calculated from the species' clutch size and spawning frequency at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], amounts to roughly 222 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = roughly 222 eggs per clutch] across a single spawning event per year [F_R_i = single spawning event per year], a value that is intermediate among small West African catfishes and reflects the constraints imposed by its modest body size and seasonal river habitat. This productivity is supported by a diet dominated by aquatic insects and benthic invertebrates, which provides the protein necessary for sustained vitellogenesis. The wet weight at puberty of 1.3 grams [Wwp = 1.3 grams] and the wet weight at birth of 0.0018 grams [Wwb = 0.0018 grams] together imply a seven-hundred-fold increase in mass from hatching to maturation, a substantial growth multiple that underscores the importance of the juvenile feeding period. Field studies have noted that individuals reaching 5 cm [Lp = 5 cm] total length are capable of spawning in their first full breeding season following maturation, though first-year spawners tend to produce smaller clutches than older, larger females.
